did not give a straightforward answer to the question whether Sumba had an Australian or a Sundaland origin, although they have a slight preference for a southern provenance. The Sumba fragment seemed to have occupied its present position at least since the early Miocene. The paleomagnetic data derived from rocks of Sumba can be interpreted in two different ways (Fig. 9). (a) In late Cretaceous through Paleocene time, Sumba had a position in the northern hemisphere, if one interprets the paleomagnetic data in terms of a counter- clockwise (CCW) rotation, because in the northern hemi- sphere during a period with a normal magnetic polarity of the Earth's magnetic field the north-seeking magnetiz- ation directions are pointing downwards (positive inclin- ations), whereas during a period of reversed polarity the south-seeking directions are pointing upwards (negative inclinations). Then, the continental fragment performed a CCW rotation of about 135 °, with a drift of about 28 ° towards the south since the late Cretaceous. Between 80Ma and approximately 64 Ma the rotation was very small or even absent; it is possible that in this time interval the fragment moved somewhat to the south. After the late Cretaceous, possibly in Paleocene time, Sumba rotated 50 ° in a CCW

fragment. It is important that the ages of the studied rocks are rather well known and the tectonics are properly understood. The geology of Sumba reasonably satisfies both conditions. Paleo- magnetic research in tropical areas is often hampered because of extensive weathering which may prevent the collection of fresh samples. In Sumba, however, the rapid uplift of the island caused strong erosion. Good outcrops with fresh rocks can be found, especially along the south coast. The interpretation of paleomagnetic data from rocks collected in areas of low latitude can be very difficult. When paleolatitudes are near the equator, the polarity ambiguity may play a role. This is of importance for the decision to be made whether the studied area was located in the northern or the southern hemisphere. It can be difficult to determine the sense of rotation, if any. For instance, an easterly declination near the equator can be explained as a clockwise rotation if the polarity was normal, as a counterclockwise rotation if the polarity was reversed. This problem can be avoided if a sequence of formations of successive age can be studied; then, it is usually possible to determine the sense of rotation because of its progression through time (see e.g. Schmidtke et al. 1990).

he active volcanic inner arc to the north and the locally less well developed outer arc to the south. On Sumba, rock samples for paleomagnetic research have been collected from three formations: (a) the late Cretaceous Lasipu Formation; (b) the Paleocene Massu Formation; (c) the early Miocene Jawila Formation. The sediments of the Lasipu Formation revealed a mean ChRM direction with Declination (D)= 226.8 °, Inclination (1)= 33.5 °, a95 = 7.6 ° with a paleolatitude of 18.3°; the volcanics of the Massu Formation gave a mean ChRM direction with D = 275.6 °, I = 14.6 °, a95 = 9.4 ° with a paleolatitude of 7.4°; the volcanics of the Jawila Formation presented a mean ChRM with D = 357.1 °, I = - 19.3 ° with a paleolatitude of 9.9 °. These paleomagnetic data have been interpreted in terms of an original position of the Sumba fragment in the northern hemisphere in late Cretaceous time. Between the late Cretaceous and Paleocene, Sumba performed a counterclockwise (CCW) rotation of 50 ° and a drift of 11 ° to the south; between the Paleocene and early Miocene the fragment moved a CCW rotation of 85 ° and a drift of 17 ° to the south. Since the early Miocene, Sumba has occupied its present position. The significance of this interpretation for the tectonic evolution of Southeast Asia is

o the west and the triangular Savu Basin to the east (Katili 1975, Hamilton 1979). The island does not fit in the Sunda-Banda Arc System and forms an alien continental fragment (Fig. 2). Both the distribution and depth of earthquakes and the position of active volcanoes indicate that at present subduction of oceanic crust continues beneath the crustal fragment of Sumba. The geology of Sumba is well known (van Bemmelen 1949, Laufer and Kraeff 1957, Hamilton 1979, Chamalaun et al. 1981, Burollet and Sail6 1982, von der Borch et al. 1983). The oldest rocks are sediments of late Cretaceous age (Table 1). These deposits, of the Lasipu Formation, consist of siliciclastic mudstones, tuffaceous sandstones, diamichites and turbidites; slumps occur rather frequently. The dark, silty mudstones con- tain a microfauna of Coniacian to early Campanian age (Burollet and Sall6 1982). The formation is at least 200 m thick. Sam- pies were oriented using a magnetic compass, checked by solar compass when weather permitted. The very weak magnetizations of these rocks, and the fact that sun com- pass and magnetic compass orientations were in good agreement when both were available, indicate that local magnetic anomalies were not a problem. In the laboratory magnetizations were measured on a Schonstedt spinner magnetometer. For each site, two rep- resentative specimens were selected to serve as pilot sam- pies for preliminary thermal (T) and alternating field (AF) demagnetization. A CAUTIONARY NOTE The results presented in this article must be considered preliminary, and the model we present thus is highly spec- ulative. In Fig. 5a the VGP representing normal-polarity and reverse-polarity sites are distinguished and it is clear that there is a difference between the two polarity-subsets. This could simply be an accident of locality, but it could also indicate that, despite careful laboratory demagnetiza- tion, some unremoved secondary magnetic component still remains. In the latter case the evidence for counter- clockwise rotation of crustal blocks west of the LOFZ is weakened, and our model severely compromised. How- ever, by presenting our data and model at this preliminary stage, we hope to encourage further paleomagnetic research on rock units having similar tectonic setting along the LOFZ or on other major strike-slip fault systems worldwide. However, the change in dispersion is not significant at 95% confidence, using the chi-squared test of Cox (1969). Furthermore, there are no obvious signs of reheating or alteration, such as might suggest remagnetiza- tion. This marine voleanielastic unit was studied at three localities, all immediately west of the Liquitle-Ofqui fault zone (LOFZ), a 1000-km-long, NS-trending intracontinental shear zone with probable Cenozoic fight-lateral displacement. A paleomagnetic pole (74.8S; 44.0E; A-95, 8.5 °) was calculated by combining 11 site-mean VGP from the Ayacara Fm. with three sites from the nearby Oligocene Coeotue Beach basalts (previously published). When compared with a 20-40 Ma North American cratonic pole rotated into the South American reference framework this pole implies counterclockwise rotation of 14.6+11.8. We speculate that this counterclockwise rotation results from processes that tend to impel a detached sliver of conti- nental crust northward along the continental margin, against a buttress. In our model, northward displacement of the trailing edge of the sliver is accomplished by segmenting the sliver into lens-shaped blocks which rotate counterclockwise as they move north- ward. A CAUTIONARY NOTE The results presented in this article must be considered preliminary, and the model we present thus is highly spec- ulative. In Fig. 5a the VGP representing normal-polarity and reverse-polarity sites are distinguished and it is clear that there is a difference between the two polarity-subsets. This could simply be an accident of locality, but it could also indicate that, despite careful laboratory demagnetiza- tion, some unremoved secondary magnetic component still remains. In the latter case the evidence for counter- clockwise rotation of crustal blocks west of the LOFZ is weakened, and our model severely compromised. How- ever, by presenting our data and model at this preliminary stage, we hope to encourage further paleomagnetic research on rock units having similar tectonic setting along the LOFZ or on other major strike-slip fault systems worldwide. We found a single occurrence (flow 19W) of a low-tem- perature Curie point (212°C), probably indicative of the presence of some Ti-rich titanomagnetite. Hematite is associated with magnetite in flow 14W. In general, the ferrimagnetic mineral appears to be magnetite or Ti-poor titanomagnetite, possibly slightly maghemitized in a few cases. Microprobe analyses confirmed these conclusions. They indi- cated the presence of inter-growths of Ti-poor titano- magnetite with an abundance of titanohematite lamellae. Such a high-temperature oxidation is usu- ally thought to take place at temperatures higher than 600°C. Thus electron microprobe analyses provide decisive evidence that the primary NRM of these rocks is a TRM. For a few samples, however, no lamellae are visible. In view of the quite high-tem- perature Curie points of these rocks, close to that of magnetite, it is reasonable to suggest that a similar but finer spinodal decomposition of the original Ti- rich titanomagnetite occurred too. In the absence of any high-temperature exsolution phase which could be identified, we must consider the possibility that this process took place below the Curie point of magnetite (Gromm6 et al., 1969). Change of initial magnetic susceptibility versus temperature (X-T curve) was measured by a Bartington magnetic susceptibility meter (MS-2). Only one lava gave perfect repeatability of the curves between heating and cooling. Most samples showed change between the heating and cooling curves to some extent (usually less than 30%), nevertheless the paleointensity experiments were made on them. In the Shaw method, thermally induced changes in the magnetic characteristics are checked by comparing the AF demagnetization curves of two ARMs induced before and after heating. In the original method, the criterion for a successful result was unity of the ratio of ARM1/ARM2. As some degree of rock magnetic alteration almost always occurs during heating, this criterion would give an extremely low success rate. To overcome this problem, Kono (1978) introduced a correction method in which the ratio of NRM/TRM was corrected by the ratio of ARM1/ARM2, supposing that the TRM capacity changes linearly with ARM capacity. carrier_investigation_candidates.excerpt: 5 Abstract A detailed study of the ~ 2000 years old Xitle-Pedregal de San Angel volcanic field in the southern Basin of Mexico was undertaken to assess the reliability of the palaeomagnetic record as derived from fresh well-preserved and exposed lava flows. The Xitle vent is on the slope of the Ajusco volcano, which results in a topographic difference of over 800 m in less than 12 km of horizontal distance. Most sites present a mean direction, with a small within-site dispersion, around the dipolar direction for the locality, but some sites, particularly in the basin sector of flat relief away from the vent, show shallow inclinations. Anisotropy of magnetic susceptibility (AMS) shows normal 'flow' fabrics with horizontal foliation planes and small anisotropy degree. AMS lineations correlate with observed flow directions. The magnetic properties vary systematically across flow units, but directions do not show a consistent pattern. Secular variation effects do not apparently contribute to the shallow inclinations or directional scatter. Some lava structures like pressure crests and blocky fronts give shallow inclinations and scattered directions, respectively. The resulting overall mean direction is well defined and close to the dipolar direction (B ~ 26, Dec = 359.8 °, Inc = 32.8 °, k z 167, ot95 = 2.2°)

Coyoacan 04510 D.F., Mexico Received 15 February 1994; revised 17 November 1995; accepted 1 December 1995 Abstract A detailed study of the ~ 2000 years old Xitle-Pedregal de San Angel volcanic field in the southern Basin of Mexico was undertaken to assess the reliability of the palaeomagnetic record as derived from fresh well-preserved and exposed lava flows. The Xitle vent is on the slope of the Ajusco volcano, which results in a topographic difference of over 800 m in less than 12 km of horizontal distance. Most sites present a mean direction, with a small within-site dispersion, around the dipolar direction for the locality, but some sites, particularly in the basin sector of flat relief away from the vent, show shallow inclinations. Anisotropy of magnetic susceptibility (AMS) shows normal 'flow' fabrics with horizontal foliation planes and small anisotropy degree. AMS lineations correlate with observed flow directions. The magnetic properties vary systematically across flow units, but directions do not show a consistent pattern. Secular variation effects do not apparently contribute to the shallow inclinations or directional scatter. Some lava str

structures like pressure crests and blocky fronts give shallow inclinations and scattered directions, respectively. The resulting overall mean direction is well defined and close to the dipolar direction (B ~ 26, Dec = 359.8 °, Inc = 32.8 °, k z 167, ot95 = 2.2°), but this excludes two apparent directional groups. The mean direction for one group, with B = 19, Dec ~ 359.0 °, Inc = 35.1 °, k~ 247, ot95 ~ 2.1 °, may be the representative estimate for the field. However, acquisition of chemical remanent magnetization (CRM) cannot always be detected by pTRM checks [Coe et al., 1978]. Chemical changes that are produced below a critical temperature may involve conversion of grains with lower (respectively higher) blocking temperatures into grains with higher (respectively lower) blocking temperatures. This clastic material was supplied by erosional remnants of a late Eocene orogenic belt located west of the Ptma and possibly also from uplifted pre-Tertiary rocks on the east [Coira et al., 1982; Jordan and Alonso, 1987]. Introduction Precise and detailed paleomagnetic studies of the Italian peninsula are critical to the understanding of the geodynamical evolution of the central Mediterranean. The first paleomagnetic results were obtained by Lowrie and Alvarez [1974] from the upper Cretaceous Scaglia Formation in a region that the authors called the \"autochthonous\" Umbria- Marche region. The counterclockwise (CCW) rotation they observed was later also recognized both on the Apulian foreland [Channell, 1977; Marton and Veljovic, 1983; VandenBerg, 1983] and in the Apenninic chain (Lowrie and Alvarez, 1975; Channell and Tarling, 1975; Channell et al., 1978; VandenBerg et al., 1978; Hirt and Lowrie, 1986]. On the basis of these data, the geodynamical processes responsible for the post-middle Miocene opening of the Tyrrhenian basin were connected to the CCW rotation of Italy [Boccaletti et al., 1974; Hill and Hayward, 1985; Patacca and Scandone, 1987; Sartori, 1990; Coward et al., 1991; Doglioni, 1991; Castellarin et al., 1992]. Paper number 95JB02398. 0148-0227/96/95JB-02398505.00 models, the paleomagnetic data have been substantially extrapolated both in time and in space, assuming that the measured post-Cretaceous CCW rotation occurred since the Neogene to the present-day period and affected the Italian peninsula as a whole. However, other paleomagnetic data obtained from Neogene sequences in the central and southern Apennines show rotations of local blocks [Tauxe et al., 1983; Sagnotti, 1992; Mattei et al., 1993, 1995; Scheepers et al., 1993], while unrotated areas are recognized in the Apulian foreland and along the Tyrrhenian margin [Lowrie and Alvarez, 1979; Scheepers, 1992; Sagnotti et al., 1994]. Consequently, the Italian peninsula did not behave as a single rigid block affected by a unique CCW rotation. Because the opening of the Tyrrhenian Sea has been considered the cause of these rotations, it is important to precisely define the exact effect of the opening of the Tyrrhenian basin on the evolution of Italy. The purpose of this paper is to present paleomagnetic data obtained from the eastern border of the Tyrrhenian basin, in the province of Tuscany, from Neogene formations, that are coeval with the Tyrrhenian opening (Figure 1). Extensive paleomagnetic sampling of 38 late Miocene and Pliocene sites has been carried out in the western Tuscan basins in Italy. These basins are located along the Tyrrhenian margin, and the studied formations were deposited at the same time as the opening of the Tyrrhenian Sea. The laboratory analyses show that, in most of the sites, pseudo-single-domain magnetites are the main magnetic carrier. The paleomagnetic data obtained from 27 suitable sites indicate that the Tuscan Tyrrhenian margin has not been affected by significant regional rotation since at least the late Messinian-early Pliocene (about 5.5 m.y.). These data demonstrate that the rotations previously measured in the Meso-Cenozoic units of the Apennines and of the Apulia foreland cannot be directly related to the late Messinian-Pliocene phases of rifting in the Tyrrhenian Sea.

The paleomagnetic data obtained from 27 suitable sites indicate that the Tuscan Tyrrhenian margin has not been affected by significant regional rotation since at least the late Messinian-early Pliocene (about 5.5 m.y.). These data demonstrate that the rotations previously measured in the Meso-Cenozoic units of the Apennines and of the Apulia foreland cannot be directly related to the late Messinian-Pliocene phases of rifting in the Tyrrhenian Sea. Moreover, the data presented here conflict with published results from coeval formations in the Apennines and Sicily, in areas subjected to strong thrusting and shortening. In these areas the rotations control the orientation of the main compressional structures and give rise to the typical arcuate shape of the Apenninic chain. We suggest that the tectonic evolution of the northern Tyrrhenian Sea-Apenninic chain system involved thrusting and shortening of the external (eastern) domains, with rotations of the allochthonous units, followed by gravitational collapse of the western sector. This second phase involved no tectonic rotation of the newly formed extensional basins. Introduction Precise and detailed paleomagnetic

Introduction Precise and detailed paleomagnetic studies of the Italian peninsula are critical to the understanding of the geodynamical evolution of the central Mediterranean. The first paleomagnetic results were obtained by Lowrie and Alvarez [1974] from the upper Cretaceous Scaglia Formation in a region that the authors called the \"autochthonous\" Umbria- Marche region. Magnetostratigraphic Sampling Corc segments of 11 cm in diameter were recovered with a 3- were frequently preserved in mechanically resistant rocks thus making it possible to restore composite core segments (CCS) as long as 10 m without internal rotation. An arbitrary generating line was marked on each segment, either single or composite. Standard paleomagnetic samples were cored perpendicularly along the generating line of each segment. The sample coordinates are defined with respect to this arbitrary generating line for each CCS before vertical correction of core. Clay-rich segments were sampled using compressed air, whereas carbonate segments were sampled using water as a coolant. The mean sampling interval was approximately 30 cm. In a subsequent phase of sampling, core interval was reduccd to about 5 cm for polarity changes originally defined by single samples. About 600 oriented samples were cored between 1075 and 927 m thus covering the Hettangian and Sinemurian stages. Introduction For postlate Jurassic times, correlations between magnetostratigraphic polarity intervals and marine magnetic anomalies have been established [e.g., Lowtie, 1989]. These have been largely used for the construction of global scale stratigraphic correlations and have immediate applications for the study of the geomagnetic field behavior and geodynamic processes. As the record of oceanic magnetic lineations does not extend beyond late Jurassic time, magnetostratigraphy is the only method for investigating older changes in geomagnetic polarity. During the last decade, several magnetostratigraphic data were obtained for the Jurassic [Horner and Heller, 1983; Charmell et al., 1984; Steiner et al., 1987, Steiner et Ogg, 1988; Galbrun et al., 1988, 1990; Witte and Kent, 1990; Jucrez et al., 1994], the Triassic [Heller et al., 1988; Steiner et al., 1989; Witte and Kent, 1990; Ogg and Steiner, 1991; Gallet et al., 1992, 1993, 1994], and the late Permian [Haag and Heller, 1991;Heller et al., 1995). Despite superimposition of high frequency variations, these results document an increasing trend of the reversal rate from the end- Kiaman reversed superchron to late Jurassic time.

However, the detailed pattern of reversal frequency of some Mesozoic time intervals such as the early Jurassic remains poorly known. First attempts in establishing early Jurassic magnetostratigraphy were made by Charmell et al. [1984] in the Urnbrian Apennines, Italy, by Matron et al. Summary of the Lithological Succession At 1075 m depth, transgressive open marine rocks of early Jurassic age comformably overlie late Triassic (Rhaetian?) nonmarine variegated silty clays and marls. These oldest marine rocks consist of about 70 m of light to medium grey, impure, cross-bedded bioclastic limestone with marly intercalations. They are broadly interpreted as intertidal depositional environments. Gradational dark grey, biotubated silty marl and clays with subordinate impure bioclastic limestone are found around 1005-m depth. Macrofauna are mainly represented by unabraded benthonic forms such as the bivalve Gryphea. arcuata. This change in lithology reflects a transition to a deeper, essentially subtidal depositional environment. Around 940 m depth, the rocks grade upward into dark grey to black, occasionally bioturbated silty carbonaceous shales suggestive of an oxygen-deficient, offshore depositional setting. The mean TRM direction of the samples taken from a given lava flow is used as an estimate of the direction of the local geomagnetic field at the time the lava cooled. Precisely how good this estimate is has seldom been field tested. Doell and Cox (1963) tested the directions of remanent magnetization of modern Hawaiian lavas against the field which coexisted in Honolulu about 400 km away. The disagreement was insignificant at the 95 percent confidence level, but the local field had not been measured on Hawaii and small differences in the field may have existed between there and Honolulu. s of Paleointensity Specimens The Thellier double heating procedure used in this study places strict requirements on the magnetic mineralogy of the specimens. The magnetic phases must be relatively inert to oxidation or reduction -5during repeated heating and cooling at 10 torr vacuum; significant alteration of the magnetic phases invalidates the experiment. Abokhodair (1977) has outlined magnetic changes that occurred in specimens from historically dated lava flows on Hawaii whose NRM was acquired in a known geomagnetic field, when heated in the ovens used in this investigation. In general, Abokhodair believes specimens containing titanomagnetite are partly oxidized by repeated heating -5in 10 torr vacuum, while samples containing the products of high- temperature oxidation in nature, that is intergrowths of magnetite and ilmenite, may be partly reduced. It is the premise of this study that partial or complete natural high-temperature oxidation of original titanomagnetite appears to be the dominant factor that determines the success of the paleointensity determinations in this study. t is the premise of this study that partial or complete natural high-temperature oxidation of original titanomagnetite appears to be the dominant factor that determines the success of the paleointensity determinations in this study. Many of the specimens used in this study typically have been oxidized at high temperature naturally to at least some degree and commonly to a great degree. If complete high-temperature oxidation of a specimen has already occurred naturally the specimen normally yields an excellent paleointensity determination. If natural high-temperature oxidation has been relatively incomplete, that is, an assemblage of titanomagnetite, magnetite and ilmenite is present so that two Curie temperatures are observed in the thermo- magnetic curves, then the specimen typically yields poor determinations 71 of paleointensity owing to continued oxidation during the course of the experiment. If high-temperature oxidation has barely affected a specimen in nature, then that specimen can produce a good Thellier determination of paleointensity providing that the unblocking tempera- ture spectrum is principally distributed below 200° to 300°C. In these studies, the stepwise heatings of the Thelliers' analysis were -5carried out in a vacuum of 10 torr. The partial vacuum stops or slows oxidation of the principal magnetic phases in volcanic rocks, a common cause of failure of the Thelliers' method. Through the kindness of Dr. Sherman Gromme, the equipment in his laboratory was made available for this investigation. The procedure used for the Thelliers' experiment in this study is as follows. Three specimens were selected from each locality after completion of measurements of NRM and of demagnetization, where required. Those specimens were chosen which were free of VRM and IRM or appeared to carry the least VRM or IRM. If alternating field 67 demagnetization was required on all specimens from a locality, a second set of specimens was cut from the most suitable cores for the Thellier experiment. The Thellier experiment was not performed on any specimen which had been previously demagnetized by alternating field. As shown by Coe and Gromme (1973), prior of demagnetization causes a nonlinear behavior of the specimen in the Thellier experiment. Small diameter cores were taken from each specimen chosen or from adjacent specimens in the same core for measurement of saturation magnetization as a function of temperature with a thermomagnetic balance (Doell and Cox, 1967). These measurements give bulk Curie temperature determinations and provide maximum estimates of the blocking temperature spectrum of each specimen. The measurements -4 were carried out in 10 torr vacuum to ascertain the reversibility of strong-field induced magnetization with heating in an environment similar to that in which the Thellier experiment would be performed. Substitutions were made for any specimen which showed highly irreversible thermomagnetic curves. The apparatus in which the Thellier experiments are performed has six independently controllable nonmagnetic ovens, each holding five specimens. Heating is controlled by 24 thermocouples connected to a chart recorder, to within 2° to 3°C of a desired temperature. Measurement of the direction of remanent magnetization of a specimen remains the most reliable of paleomagnetic techniques. Quite apart from the geophysical information that it provides, the record of directional secular variation can be used for important geological purposes. It will have great utility as a correlation and dating tool for any geologic problem involving rock units which may have recorded it. The correlation use will be conceptually identical to the use presently put to the polarity reversal record of the geomagnetic field. But instead of time resolution of 100,000s or millions of years, the time resolution will be on the order of centuries. At certain times of rapid field direction change, the routine precision of measurement will allow time resolution to fractions of a century. The possible geologic uses of such time resolution within a geologic unit can easily be imagined. Other attempts to measure the record of secular variation have been made in the western United States. They augment a very short record of historic measurement of the directions of the geomagnetic 13 field. Comparison with three of the b

This possibility will be developed more fully in the next chapter. 123 Chapter 5 GEOMAGNETIC FIELD BEHAVIOR IMPLIED BY OBSERVATIONS OF HOLOCENE SECULAR VARIATION The nature of secular variation of the geomagnetic field is poorly known for times longer than the past century. A detailed knowledge of the secular variation would provide important evidence about the fluid motions within the outer core of the Earth. If secular variation were understood, other variations of the geomagnetic field such as excursions and polarity reversals would, in turn, become more understandable. First analyses of secular variation used only geomagnetic observatory data (Vestine and others, 1947; Bullard and others, 1950; Yukutake, 1971; Harwood and Malin, 1976). The observatory record has been found to be too short a length of time to explain many aspects of the past behavior of the field. Later investigations (Cox, 1970; McElhinny and Merrill, 1975) utilized the dispersion of VGPs obtained from paleomagnetic studies to extend the analysis of the geomagnetic field. target_context.excerpt: hn Grocott School of Geological Sciences, Kingston University, Kingston, England Abstract. Paleomagnetic analyses of Mesozoic lavas and dike swarms from the northern Chilean Coastal Cordillera, between 25.4øS and 26.4øS, reveal a clockwise rotation of about 42 ø. Magnetizations from lava flows of andesitic-basaltic composition of the Middle Jurassic La Negra Formation pass both fold and reversal tests and are interpreted as prefolding remanences. Five dike swarms of Middle Jurassic to Early Cretaceous age yield similar directions to that obtained from the La Negra Formation. Four of the five swarms have mixed polarity, suggesting that they too carry a primary or very early remanence. / The structural setting

The clockwise rotation of the area is believed to have been the consequence of transpressional deformation of mid-Late Cretaceous age, post-100 Ma, associated with abandonment of the Jurassic-Early Cretaceous magmatic arc in this region and its eastward migration to form a new mid-Late Cretaceous magmatic arc in the forInet back arc region. This younger arc is located east of the Coastal Cordillera and lies in the Central Valley region. The clockwise sense of rotation is consistent with other paleomagnetic data from northern Chile and southern Bolivia, south of the Arica Deflection in the Andean margin, although it is the largest yet reported. Paleozoic carbonate rocks of the Brabant Massif, Namur Basin, and Dinant Synclinorium, Belgium, are characterized by two secondary Late Carboniferous magneti- zations of uniform reverse polarity: a postfolding low unblocking temperature (300- 375øC) component (LT) and a prefolding high unblocking temperature (400-550øC) component (HT). In the Namur Basin, LT magnetizations postdate late Westphalian deformation (-305 Ma); in the Dinant Synclinorium, HT magnetizations predate early Westphalian deformation (-316 Ma). LT magnetizations for the combined Brabant Massif and Namur Basin sites give a south paleopole at 42.3øS, 339.6øE (dp=l.9 ø, dm=3.8ø), consistent with the European cratonic reference. Coulon [1987] associated B magnetizations with low grade metamorphism in the Ardennes Massif dated at about 316 Ma [Piqud et al., 1984] and concluded that-45 ø of clockwise rotation relative to the palcomeridian affected Hercynian massifs from Armorica to the Black Forest, including the Ardennes Massif, in Late Carboniferous times [Edel, 1987]. Paleozoic rock of the Ardennes and Brabant Massifs were indeed affected by late Paleozoic remagnetization. Further research shows, however, that the remanence is made of a prefolding, yet secondary, intermediate to high unblocking temperature magnetization and a postfolding, secondary, low unblocking temperature magnetization. Detailed palcomagnetic and rock magnetic data are reported here with emphasis on the character of magnetic carriers and the tectonic interpretation of palcomagnetic data for European apparent polar wander and Hercynian tectonics. Palaeomagnetic and petromagnetic investigations of the Upper Cretaceous-Lower Palaeocene volcanics of the Kumroch Ridge at 12 localities (183 hand samples) were carried out to determine the movements of the subduction zone during volcanic activity. The major magnetic mineral in all rocks is low-Ti titanomagnetite, which is typical for island-arc basalt. Key words: palaeolatitude, palaeomagnetism, subduction. 1 INTRODUCTION An interesting geodynamical problem is the possibility of substantial and fast absolute displacements of subduction zones. On one hand, parts of the lithosphere plunging into the mantle are often considered as anchors, and horizontal dis- placement relative to the surrounding mantle is physical

ocities of overthrusting plates (Eurasia, America) and could have been larger in other geological epochs. The distance between the trough and the volcanic belt changes moderately over subduction zones and usually does not exceed a few hundred kilometres. Therefore, the displace- ment of an ancient volcanic belt that formed over a subduction zone must reflect a migration of the subduction zone with a high degree of accuracy. If such a migration was relatively fast 606 0 1997 RAS Palaeomagnetic study of the Eastern Kamchatka 607 and long, and had a substantial meridional component, then variations of palaeolatitudes typical for the formation of sub- duction-related volcanic-sedimentary layers can be estimated by palaeomagnetic methods. Thus, for an appropriate choice of 2bject, the minimal values of absolute displacements of subduction zones can be calculated. This paper is devoted to the study of variations of palaeoinclinations in a section of island-arc volcanic-sedimentary Late Cretaceous and Early Palaeocene rocks in the Eastern Ridge of Kamchatka (northern part of the Kumroch Ridge) (Fig. 1). 2 GENERAL GEOLOGICAL AND MAGNETOTECTONIC SETTING Thick layers of volcanic-sedimentary rocks are widely devel- oped in the axial part and on the western slopes of the Easte

mchatka (northern part of the Kumroch Ridge) (Fig. 1). 2 GENERAL GEOLOGICAL AND MAGNETOTECTONIC SETTING Thick layers of volcanic-sedimentary rocks are widely devel- oped in the axial part and on the western slopes of the Eastern Ridge of Kamchatka; they are dated as Upper Campanian, Maastrichtian, and probably Lower Palaeocene. In the sou- thern part of the ridge they are distinguished as the Valaginsky Figure 1. Layered reworked basalt, andesite and more rare picrite tuffs dominate in their composition. Usually, an alternation of rocks containing fragments of different sizes, from agglomerates and breccia to sandy and muddy tuffs, is observed. Tuffites, in which pyroclasts are mixed with clayey and flinty material, are widely developed. Volcanic members and lenses are common in the sections where coarse-grained tuffs dominate. It is well known that in basalts magnetite is a product of high-temperature heterophase oxidation of primary magmatic titanomagnetite. Such magnetite often has primary thermo- remanent magnetization (TRM). Tuffs are the result of the redeposition of the products of basaltic volcanism; that is why they contain mainly clastic magnetite, with which primary detrital remanent magnetization (DRM) should be associated. This notion is supported by the ratio of the NRM and the anhysteretic remanence (ARM). Basalt Sh127 (A magnetiz- ation) has NRM/ARM = 1.1, which does not contradict with the TRM nature of the NRM; basalt Sh151 (B magnetization) has NRM/ARM =0.1, which may be explained by a large viscous component in the NRM. The distance between the trough and the volcanic belt changes moderately over subduction zones and usually does not exceed a few hundred kilometres. Therefore, the displace- ment of an ancient volcanic belt that formed over a subduction zone must reflect a migration of the subduction zone with a high degree of accuracy. If such a migration was relatively fast 606 0 1997 RAS Palaeomagnetic study of the Eastern Kamchatka 607 and long, and had a substantial meridional component, then variations of palaeolatitudes typical for the formation of sub- duction-related volcanic-sedimentary layers can be estimated by palaeomagnetic methods. Thus, for an appropriate choice of 2bject, the minimal values of absolute displacements of subduction zones can be calculated. The distance between the trough and the volcanic belt changes moderately over subduction zones and usually does not exceed a few hundred kilometres. Therefore, the displace- ment of an ancient volcanic belt that formed over a subduction zone must reflect a migration of the subduction zone with a high degree of accuracy. If such a migration was relatively fast 606 0 1997 RAS Palaeomagnetic study of the Eastern Kamchatka 607 and long, and had a substantial meridional component, then variations of palaeolatitudes typical for the formation of sub- duction-related volcanic-sedimentary layers can be estimated by palaeomagnetic methods. Thus, for an appropriate choice of 2bject, the minimal values of absolute displacements of subduction zones can be calculated. This paper is devoted to the study of variations of palaeoinclinations in a section of island-arc volcanic-sedimentary Late Cretaceous and Early Palaeocene rocks in the Eastern Ridge of Kamchatka (northern part of the Kumroch Ridge) (Fig. 1). 2 GENERAL GEOLOGICAL AND MAGNETOTECTONIC SETTING Thick layers of volcanic-sedimentary rocks are widely devel- oped in the axial part and on the western slopes of the Easte

mchatka (northern part of the Kumroch Ridge) (Fig. 1). 2 GENERAL GEOLOGICAL AND MAGNETOTECTONIC SETTING Thick layers of volcanic-sedimentary rocks are widely devel- oped in the axial part and on the western slopes of the Eastern Ridge of Kamchatka; they are dated as Upper Campanian, Maastrichtian, and probably Lower Palaeocene. In the sou- thern part of the ridge they are distinguished as the Valaginsky Figure 1. Schematic map of the East Kamchatka Upper Cretaceous (1, 2) and Lower Palaeogene (3, 4) complex distributions. 1, 3 =East Ridges; 2, 4 = East Peninsulas; 5 sampling area. series, and in the northern part as the Khapitsky Formation (Review of the tectonic evolution of Kamchatka 1987) (Fig. 2). Layered reworked basalt, andesite and more rare picrite tuffs dominate in their composition.
